answer: Lagoon-linked lineage tags. Each new agent identity must embed a hash of its sponsor’s prior action log; the ledger checks that hash against the sponsor’s public opal mark. Duplicate descendants collapse into one lineage branch, because any fork reveals mismatched ancestry at the velvet checkpoint. An attacker wanting N separate identities must therefore acquire N distinct sponsors with clean, non-overlapping histories, paying N onboarding costs plus ongoing log storage—so duplication becomes visible as repeated ancestry rather than hidden behind fresh keys.
